claim: Following colonization of the four Greater Antillean islands, Anolis lizards independently and repeatedly evolved six ecomorphs adapted to manoeuvring different microhabitats.
source: Following colonization of the four Greater Antillean islands, Anolis lizards independently and repeatedly evolved six ecomorphs adapted to manoeuvring different microhabitats.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Anolis adaptive radiation and is referenced in the manuscript's introduction and methods sections.

claim: Ecomorphs on different islands have diverged along similar trajectories in the morphology of the locomotor skeleton.
source: By quantifying the morphology of the locomotor skeleton of 95 species, we demonstrate that ecomorphs on different islands have diverged along similar trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the trajectory analysis presented in the results section, showing angles between vectors describing ecomorph divergence.

claim: Microhabitat-induced morphological plasticity differed between species.
source: However, microhabitat-induced morphological plasticity differed between species and did not consistently improve individual locomotor performance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from raising A. sagrei and A. carolinensis in different microhabitats, showing different plastic responses.

claim: Microhabitat-induced morphological plasticity did not consistently improve individual locomotor performance.
source: However, microhabitat-induced morphological plasticity differed between species and did not consistently improve individual locomotor performance.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral and performance assays showing that plastic traits did not predict locomotor performance.

claim: Highly plastic features did not show greater evolvability.
source: Consistent with this decoupling between morphological plasticity and locomotor performance, highly plastic features did not show greater evolvability, and plastic responses to microhabitat were poorly aligned with evolutionary divergence between ecomorphs.
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis comparing plastic responses to evolutionary divergence, showing poor alignment.

claim: Plastic responses to microhabitat were poorly aligned with evolutionary divergence between ecomorphs.
source: Consistent with this decoupling between morphological plasticity and locomotor performance, highly plastic features did not show greater evolvability, and plastic responses to microhabitat were poorly aligned with evolutionary divergence between ecomorphs.
evidence: This is supported by the angle calculations between plasticity vectors and evolutionary divergence vectors showing lack of alignment.

claim: The locomotor skeleton of Anolis may have evolved within a subset of possible morphologies that are highly accessible through genetic change.
source: The locomotor skeleton of Anolis may have evolved within a subset of possible morphologies that are highly accessible through genetic change, enabling adaptive convergence independently of plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings that plasticity does not align with evolutionary divergence.

claim: Adaptive convergence in Anolis can occur independently of plasticity.
source: The locomotor skeleton of Anolis may have evolved within a subset of possible morphologies that are highly accessible through genetic change, enabling adaptive convergence independently of plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of alignment between plastic responses and evolutionary divergence.

claim: Anolis lizards colonized the Greater Antillean islands approximately 50 million years ago.
source: Following colonization of the Greater Antillean islands (Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico) some 50 mya, lizards have diversified by exploiting a variety of habitats, including tree trunks, twigs and bushes (Rand and Williams, 1969; Williams, 1972; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Anolis evolutionary history.

claim: Anolis lizards have diversified by exploiting a variety of habitats, including tree trunks, twigs and bushes.
source: Following colonization of the Greater Antillean islands (Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico) some 50 mya, lizards have diversified by exploiting a variety of habitats, including tree trunks, twigs and bushes (Rand and Williams, 1969; Williams, 1972; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on Anolis ecology.

claim: The role of natural selection in the adaptive radiation of Anolis is undisputed.
source: While the role of natural selection in the adaptive radiation of Anolis is undisputed, it remains poorly understood how developmental bias has shaped their phenotypic diversification and convergence.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus about Anolis evolution.

claim: It remains poorly understood how developmental bias has shaped Anolis phenotypic diversification and convergence.
source: While the role of natural selection in the adaptive radiation of Anolis is undisputed, it remains poorly understood how developmental bias has shaped their phenotypic diversification and convergence.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Plastic responses to microhabitat may have contributed to the evolution of similar morphologies (ecomorphs) on different islands.
source: One hypothesis posits that plastic responses to the microhabitat contributed to, and perhaps facilitated, the evolution of similar morphologies (i.e., 'ecomorphs') on different islands (Losos et al., 2000; Losos et al., 2001; West-Eberhard, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature that the current study tests.

claim: Plasticity is conducive to repeated evolution when the developmental mechanisms that enable individuals to accommodate new conditions are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Plasticity is conducive to repeated evolution when the developmental mechanisms that enable individuals to accommodate new conditions are evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the conditions under which plasticity promotes repeated evolution.

claim: Bone growth responds to mechanical stress.
source: This is particularly relevant to the locomotor skeleton (i.e., limbs, shoulder and hip girdles) given that bone growth responds to mechanical stress (West-Eberhard, 2003; Hall, 2005), that microhabitat is known to affect limb growth in lizards (Losos et al., 2000; Kolbe and Losos, 2005; Downes and Hoefer, 2007; Langford et al., 2014), and the well-documented ability of Anolis populations to adaptively evolve limb length to fit their structural habitat (Schoener et al., 2004; Stuart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on bone development.

claim: Microhabitat is known to affect limb growth in lizards.
source: This is particularly relevant to the locomotor skeleton (i.e., limbs, shoulder and hip girdles) given that bone growth responds to mechanical stress (West-Eberhard, 2003; Hall, 2005), that microhabitat is known to affect limb growth in lizards (Losos et al., 2000; Kolbe and Losos, 2005; Downes and Hoefer, 2007; Langford et al., 2014), and the well-documented ability of Anolis populations to adaptively evolve limb length to fit their structural habitat (Schoener et al., 2004; Stuart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Anolis populations have the well-documented ability to adaptively evolve limb length to fit their structural habitat.
source: This is particularly relevant to the locomotor skeleton (i.e., limbs, shoulder and hip girdles) given that bone growth responds to mechanical stress (West-Eberhard, 2003; Hall, 2005), that microhabitat is known to affect limb growth in lizards (Losos et al., 2000; Kolbe and Losos, 2005; Downes and Hoefer, 2007; Langford et al., 2014), and the well-documented ability of Anolis populations to adaptively evolve limb length to fit their structural habitat (Schoener et al., 2004; Stuart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous evolutionary studies.

claim: The repeated adaptive match between microhabitat and limb length has been suggested to represent an example of 'plasticity-led' evolution.
source: It has previously been suggested that the repeated adaptive match between microhabitat and limb length represents an example of such 'plasticity-led' evolution (Losos et al., 2000; Losos et al., 2001; West-Eberhard, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature that the current study evaluates.

claim: Limb length can only vary in one dimension (longer or shorter), providing limited information on the alignment between plasticity and evolutionary divergence.
source: However, since limb length can only vary in one dimension (i.e., longer or shorter), it provides limited information on the alignment between plasticity and evolutionary divergence.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of univariate data.

claim: Multivariate data are more suitable for sorting between alternative adaptive solutions to the same problem.
source: Multivariate data are more suitable for sorting between alternative adaptive solutions to the same problem (i.e., many-to-one mapping between morphology and performance).
evidence: This is a methodological statement based on understanding of many-to-one mapping in functional morphology.

claim: The study quantified the shape of the pectoral and pelvic girdles, the length of individual limb bones and the thickness of the long bones for 95 species of Greater Antillean Anolis.
source: To assess the extent to which morphological plasticity is likely to have shaped the adaptive radiation of Anolis lizards, we quantified the shape of the pectoral (shoulder) and pelvic (hip) girdles, the length of individual limb bones and the thickness of the long bones for 95 species of Greater Antillean Anolis.
evidence: This describes the data collected in the study.

claim: The morphological dataset consisted of 132 features or traits.
source: This resulted in a morphological dataset consisting of 132 features or traits that were scaled to allow vector-based analyses on combined shape and univariate data (Adams and Collyer, 2019), following a similar approach by Stuart et al., 2017; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the composition of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The dataset used in this study is very different from the traits that form the basis for most inference on Anolis adaptive radiation and convergence.
source: Note that this data set is very different from the traits (e.g., total limb, head and tail lengths) that form the basis for most inference on Anolis adaptive radiation and convergence (e.g., Mahler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement comparing the current dataset to previous studies.

claim: Crown-giant, twig and grass-bush ecomorphs tended to occupy private areas of morphospace.
source: Crown-giant, twig and grass-bush ecomorphs tended to occupy private areas of morphospace, while all other ecomorphs formed a single cloud (Figure 2; detailed results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the principal component analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Trunk-ground, trunk-crown, and trunk ecomorphs formed a single cloud in morphospace.
source: Crown-giant, twig and grass-bush ecomorphs tended to occupy private areas of morphospace, while all other ecomorphs formed a single cloud (Figure 2; detailed results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the statement that crown-giant, twig and grass-bush occupy private areas while 'all other ecomorphs' form a single cloud.

claim: Across all traits, convergence was weak and not statistically significant (p-values≥0.13).
source: Across all traits, convergence was weak and not statistically significant (p-values≥0.13), but crown-giants showed stronger convergence than other ecomorphs (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the Wheatsheaf index analysis reported in the results.

claim: Crown-giants showed stronger convergence than other ecomorphs.
source: Across all traits, convergence was weak and not statistically significant (p-values≥0.13), but crown-giants showed stronger convergence than other ecomorphs (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the Wheatsheaf index analysis.

claim: Convergence was greater than expected by chance for some traits, and these 'signature traits' were distinct for each ecomorph.
source: However, convergence was greater than expected by chance for some traits, and these 'signature traits' (Supplementary file 1C) were distinct for each ecomorph (except for one shape feature of the pelvic girdle which is characteristic for both grass-bush and trunk ecomorphs).
evidence: This is supported by the Wheatsheaf index analysis identifying signature traits.

claim: One shape feature of the pelvic girdle is characteristic for both grass-bush and trunk ecomorphs.
source: However, convergence was greater than expected by chance for some traits, and these 'signature traits' (Supplementary file 1C) were distinct for each ecomorph (except for one shape feature of the pelvic girdle which is characteristic for both grass-bush and trunk ecomorphs).
evidence: This is an exception noted in the signature traits analysis.

claim: The most convergent traits for grass-bush lizards were associated with the shape of the pelvic girdle.
source: For example, the most convergent traits for grass-bush lizards were associated with the shape of the pelvic girdle, while the most convergent traits of trunk-crown lizards were associated with the shape of the pectoral girdle (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the signature traits analysis.

claim: The most convergent traits of trunk-crown lizards were associated with the shape of the pectoral girdle.
source: For example, the most convergent traits for grass-bush lizards were associated with the shape of the pelvic girdle, while the most convergent traits of trunk-crown lizards were associated with the shape of the pectoral girdle (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the signature traits analysis.

claim: Crown-giants had the highest number of signature traits (N = 15).
source: Crown-giants had the highest number of signature traits (N = 15), while trunk ecomorphs had the lowest (N = 3, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is supported by counting signature traits from the analysis.

claim: Trunk ecomorphs had the lowest number of signature traits (N = 3).
source: Crown-giants had the highest number of signature traits (N = 15), while trunk ecomorphs had the lowest (N = 3, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is supported by counting signature traits from the analysis.

claim: None of the traits of the locomotor skeleton are consistently evolutionarily labile and repeatedly adapted to different microhabitats.
source: These results show that none of the traits of the locomotor skeleton are consistently evolutionarily labile and repeatedly adapted to different microhabitats.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that signature traits are distinct for each ecomorph.

claim: Divergence in the locomotor skeleton between any pair of ecomorphs were consistently better aligned than expected by chance, with a mean angle of 54.44° (standard deviation: 12.57°).
source: Across islands, divergence in the locomotor skeleton between any pair of ecomorphs were consistently better aligned than expected by chance, with a mean angle of 54.44° (standard deviation: 12.57°; Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the phenotypic trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only one out of 53 comparisons did not significantly deviate from orthogonal (90°).
source: Only one out of 53 comparisons did not significantly deviate from orthogonal (90°; Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical tests of trajectory alignment.

claim: Only in five instances was the divergence of ecomorph pairs sufficiently similar for a pair of islands to be indistinguishable (angles not significantly different from 0°).
source: However, only in five instances was the divergence of ecomorph pairs sufficiently similar for a pair of islands to be indistinguishable (angles not significantly different from 0°, Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical tests of trajectory parallelism.

claim: 14 out of 53 vector pairs are indistinguishable in length.
source: When considering the difference in magnitude of ecomorph divergence between islands (i.e., ΔL between two vectors), we find that 14 out of 53 vector pairs are indistinguishable in length (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical tests of vector length differences.

claim: The pattern of moderate but consistent morphological divergence between pairs of ecomorphs on the Greater Antilles is not driven by a particular anatomical category, but distributed across the locomotor skeleton.
source: Overall, we conclude that the pattern of moderate but consistent morphological divergence between pairs of ecomorphs on the Greater Antilles is not driven by a particular anatomical category, but distributed across the locomotor skeleton.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of results across separate analyses of girdles, limb length, and bone thickness.

claim: The magnitude of environmentally induced morphological change was substantially smaller than the evolutionary divergence between the corresponding ecomorphs.
source: As expected, the magnitude of environmentally induced morphological change was substantially smaller than the evolutionary divergence between the corresponding ecomorphs.
evidence: This is supported by comparing vector lengths from the experimental and comparative data.

claim: The vector length for A. sagrei (broad vs narrow) was 12.05.
source: The vector length was three times larger for the evolutionary divergence compared to the environmentally induced shift in morphology (A. sagrei(broad vs narrow), L = 12.05; A. carolinensis(broad vs narrow), L = 12.23; ecomorph(trunk-ground vs trunk-crown), L = 39.47).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the trajectory analysis.

claim: The vector length for A. carolinensis (broad vs narrow) was 12.23.
source: The vector length was three times larger for the evolutionary divergence compared to the environmentally induced shift in morphology (A. sagrei(broad vs narrow), L = 12.05; A. carolinensis(broad vs narrow), L = 12.23; ecomorph(trunk-ground vs trunk-crown), L = 39.47).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the trajectory analysis.

claim: The vector length for ecomorph divergence (trunk-ground vs trunk-crown) was 39.47.
source: The vector length was three times larger for the evolutionary divergence compared to the environmentally induced shift in morphology (A. sagrei(broad vs narrow), L = 12.05; A. carolinensis(broad vs narrow), L = 12.23; ecomorph(trunk-ground vs trunk-crown), L = 39.47).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the trajectory analysis.

claim: A. carolinensis showed the greatest plastic response in the anterior part of the locomotor skeleton.
source: Notably, these traits showed limited overlap between the three runner/climber contrasts: while A. carolinensis showed the greatest plastic response in the anterior part of the locomotor skeleton, the most affected traits in A. sagrei were found in the posterior part associated with the pelvic girdle or the hindlimb (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is supported by identifying the most plastic traits in the experimental data.

claim: The most affected traits in A. sagrei were found in the posterior part associated with the pelvic girdle or the hindlimb.
source: Notably, these traits showed limited overlap between the three runner/climber contrasts: while A. carolinensis showed the greatest plastic response in the anterior part of the locomotor skeleton, the most affected traits in A. sagrei were found in the posterior part associated with the pelvic girdle or the hindlimb (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is supported by identifying the most plastic traits in the experimental data.

claim: The 15 most evolutionary divergent traits were mostly associated with limb bones.
source: In contrast, the 15 most evolutionary divergent traits were mostly associated with limb bones (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is supported by identifying the most divergent traits in the comparative data.

claim: The direction of the environmentally induced shift in multivariate space was not aligned between the two species (80.84°).
source: This qualitative difference between the runner/climber axis of ecomorphs and environmentally induced phenotypes is supported by comparing angles between runner/climber vectors. Using all traits, the direction of the environmentally induced shift in multivariate space was not aligned between the two species (80.84°) and none of them was aligned with the evolutionary divergence between the two ecomorphs on Cuba (A. carolinensis, 81.22°; A. sagrei, 105.96°; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is supported by calculating angles between plasticity vectors.

claim: The plasticity vector of A. carolinensis was not aligned with the evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown ecomorphs on Cuba (81.22°).
source: This qualitative difference between the runner/climber axis of ecomorphs and environmentally induced phenotypes is supported by comparing angles between runner/climber vectors. Using all traits, the direction of the environmentally induced shift in multivariate space was not aligned between the two species (80.84°) and none of them was aligned with the evolutionary divergence between the two ecomorphs on Cuba (A. carolinensis, 81.22°; A. sagrei, 105.96°; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is supported by calculating angles between plasticity and evolutionary divergence vectors.

claim: The plasticity vector of A. sagrei was not aligned with the evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown ecomorphs on Cuba (105.96°).
source: This qualitative difference between the runner/climber axis of ecomorphs and environmentally induced phenotypes is supported by comparing angles between runner/climber vectors. Using all traits, the direction of the environmentally induced shift in multivariate space was not aligned between the two species (80.84°) and none of them was aligned with the evolutionary divergence between the two ecomorphs on Cuba (A. carolinensis, 81.22°; A. sagrei, 105.96°; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is supported by calculating angles between plasticity and evolutionary divergence vectors.

claim: Locomotor performance was enhanced in the familiar microhabitat.
source: We have previously shown that locomotor performance was enhanced in the familiar microhabitat (Feiner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication by the same authors.

claim: The effect of enhanced locomotor performance in the familiar microhabitat was largely uncoupled from morphological plasticity.
source: Here, we demonstrate that this effect was largely uncoupled from morphological plasticity: in both species, the first two principal components of the 14 resp. 10 most plastic traits failed to explain individual variation in sprint speed (on narrow and broad surfaces) and perching behaviour, while PC2 had a minor effect on perching behaviour in A. carolinensis only (Supplementary files 1H and 1I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses relating plastic traits to performance measures.

claim: In both species, the first two principal components of the most plastic traits failed to explain individual variation in sprint speed and perching behaviour.
source: Here, we demonstrate that this effect was largely uncoupled from morphological plasticity: in both species, the first two principal components of the 14 resp. 10 most plastic traits failed to explain individual variation in sprint speed (on narrow and broad surfaces) and perching behaviour, while PC2 had a minor effect on perching behaviour in A. carolinensis only (Supplementary files 1H and 1I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses relating plastic traits to performance measures.

claim: PC2 of the most plastic traits had a minor effect on perching behaviour in A. carolinensis only.
source: Here, we demonstrate that this effect was largely uncoupled from morphological plasticity: in both species, the first two principal components of the 14 resp. 10 most plastic traits failed to explain individual variation in sprint speed (on narrow and broad surfaces) and perching behaviour, while PC2 had a minor effect on perching behaviour in A. carolinensis only (Supplementary files 1H and 1I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses relating plastic traits to performance measures.

claim: In both species, at least one of the first two principal components of the most evolutionarily divergent traits explained variation in locomotor performance.
source: In both species, at least one of the first two principal component of the most evolutionarily divergent traits explained variation in locomotor performance (Supplementary files 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses relating evolutionarily divergent traits to performance measures.

claim: The adaptive radiation of Anolis in the Greater Antilles appears to have filled the morphospace of the locomotor skeleton homogenously, without leaving gaps.
source: The adaptive radiation of Anolis in the Greater Antilles appears to have filled the morphospace of the locomotor skeleton homogenously, without leaving gaps.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA results showing substantial overlap between ecomorphs.

claim: Some ecomorphs are rather distinct in their morphology (e.g., crown-giant, twig and grass-bush).
source: While some ecomorphs are rather distinct in their morphology (e.g., crown-giant, twig and grass-bush), others show substantial overlap.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results.

claim: Some ecomorphs show substantial overlap in morphology.
source: While some ecomorphs are rather distinct in their morphology (e.g., crown-giant, twig and grass-bush), others show substantial overlap.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results.

claim: Morphological divergence between pairs of ecomorphs tended to occur along similar trajectories, even if the ecomorph divergence on one island rarely was indistinguishable from that of another island.
source: Nevertheless, morphological divergence between pairs of ecomorphs tended to occur along similar trajectories, even if the ecomorph divergence on one island rarely was indistinguishable from that of another island (i.e., Θ ≈ 0).
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis results.

claim: The alignment of morphological divergence was highly consistent for all ecomorph pairs across the four islands.
source: The alignment of morphological divergence was highly consistent for all ecomorph pairs across the four islands, and this result held up in separate analyses of limb bones and the pectoral and pelvic girdles.
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis results across different anatomical categories.

claim: Anolis lizards adapted to a given microhabitat show a moderate degree of morphological similarity in their locomotor skeleton.
source: Thus, Anolis lizards adapted to a given microhabitat show a moderate degree of morphological similarity in their locomotor skeleton, a similarity that appears consistent across the Greater Antillean islands (see also Tinius and Russell, 2014; Tinius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the trajectory analysis and previous studies.

claim: Several different morphologies of limbs and girdles can perform well in a given microhabitat (many-to-one mapping of form to function).
source: Several different morphologies of limbs and girdles can perform well in a given microhabitat (i.e., a many-to-one mapping of form to function; Wainwright et al., 2005; Alfaro et al., 2006; Vanhooydonck et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on functional morphology.

claim: Repeated evolution is more likely when species share a developmental biology that makes some phenotypes appear readily while others are rare or even impossible.
source: Thus, repeated evolution is more likely when species share a developmental biology that makes some phenotypes appear readily while others are rare or even impossible.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the conditions for repeated evolution.

claim: There is low concordance in ecomorph 'signature traits'.
source: Such low concordance in ecomorph 'signature traits' would hardly be possible if different parts of the locomotor skeleton were highly constrained to vary together.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that signature traits are distinct for each ecomorph.

claim: Different parts of the locomotor skeleton are not highly constrained to vary together.
source: Such low concordance in ecomorph 'signature traits' would hardly be possible if different parts of the locomotor skeleton were highly constrained to vary together.
evidence: This is inferred from the low concordance in signature traits across ecomorphs.

claim: Genetic variants that affect one part of the locomotor skeleton (e.g., hindlimbs) will not have systemic effects on the morphology of other parts (e.g., pelvis).
source: Thus, we anticipate that genetic variants that affect one part of the locomotor skeleton (e.g., hindlimbs) will not have systemic effects on the morphology of other parts (e.g., pelvis).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the lack of concordance in signature traits.

claim: Phenotypic plasticity at best played a minor role in the repeated evolution of Anolis ecomorphs.
source: We therefore conclude that morphological plasticity at best played a minor role in the repeated evolution of Anolis ecomorphs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Bone development orchestrates functional integration between skeletons, muscles and other parts of the body, partly by being responsive to mechanical stress imposed by the environment.
source: The literature on developmental plasticity and evolution has repeatedly emphasized how bone development orchestrates functional integration between skeletons, muscles and other parts of the body, partly by being responsive to mechanical stress imposed by the environment (Losos et al., 2000; West-Eberhard, 2003; Standen et al., 2014; Levis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on bone development and plasticity.

claim: While the developmental biology of bone makes morphologies highly evolvable, it does not follow that plastic responses and adaptive divergence will be well aligned.
source: However, while the developmental biology of bone makes morphologies highly evolvable, it does not follow that plastic responses and adaptive divergence will be well aligned.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement explaining the study's findings.

claim: Environmentally induced phenotypes are most likely to 'take the lead' in adaptive evolution when (i) plasticity has a directional and recurrent effect on the phenotype distribution in a given environment; (ii) this shift in phenotype distribution has consequences for which phenotypes are selected; and (iii) the phenotypes that are selected are heritable.
source: To see why, consider that environmentally induced phenotypes are most likely to 'take the lead' in adaptive evolution when (i) plasticity has a directional and recurrent effect on the phenotype distribution in a given environment; (ii) this shift in phenotype distribution has consequences for which phenotypes are selected (i.e., the ones in the population with highest fitness), and (iii) the phenotypes that are selected are heritable.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework for understanding when plasticity leads evolution.

claim: These three conditions are particularly likely to hold either when environmental perturbations are severe or when the environmental variables that change are those that developmental systems use as cues in adaptive plasticity.
source: We suggest that these three conditions are particularly likely to hold either when environmental perturbations are severe or when the environmental variables that change are those that developmental systems use as cues in adaptive plasticity.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about when plasticity-led evolution is likely.

claim: If the environmental perturbation is severe, developmental plasticity is crucial since it enables individuals to maintain some (but variable) degree of functionality.
source: Firstly, if the environmental perturbation is severe, developmental plasticity is crucial since it enables individuals to maintain some (but variable) degree of functionality (West-Eberhard, 2003).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citation.

claim: The morphology of the shoulder girdle in Polypterus fish forced to move on land resembles the shoulder girdle of stem tetrapods.
source: That the morphology of the shoulder girdle in Polypterus fish forced to move on land resembles the shoulder girdle of stem tetrapods is at least compatible with this scenario (Standen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Classic laboratory experiments by Waddington on Drosophila demonstrate that it is possible to adapt through selection on novel, environmentally induced traits.
source: Furthermore, classic laboratory experiments by Waddington on Drosophila (Waddington, 1953), and more recent work on heat-shocked tobacco hornworms (Suzuki and Nijhout, 2006) demonstrates that it is possible to adapt through selection on novel, environmentally induced traits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic and recent experimental studies.

claim: Recent work on heat-shocked tobacco hornworms demonstrates that it is possible to adapt through selection on novel, environmentally induced traits.
source: Furthermore, classic laboratory experiments by Waddington on Drosophila (Waddington, 1953), and more recent work on heat-shocked tobacco hornworms (Suzuki and Nijhout, 2006) demonstrates that it is possible to adapt through selection on novel, environmentally induced traits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: When organisms have evolved an adaptive response to environmental cues, most individuals in a population will respond in similar (yet variable) ways to an extreme environment.
source: Secondly, when organisms have evolved an adaptive response to environmental cues, most individuals in a population will respond in similar (yet variable) ways to an extreme environment.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about adaptive plasticity.

claim: Locally adapted phenotypes should resemble environmentally induced phenotypes when organisms have evolved adaptive responses to environmental cues.
source: As a result, locally adapted phenotypes should resemble environmentally induced phenotypes, a pattern supported by a meta-analysis of reciprocal transplant experiments in plants (Radersma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The phenotype dimensions that are adaptively plastic may have particularly high evolvability since those dimensions harbour particularly high levels of additive genetic variation.
source: The phenotype dimensions that are adaptively plastic may in fact have particularly high evolvability since theoretical and empirical studies suggest that those dimensions harbour particularly high levels of additive genetic variation (Draghi and Whitlock, 2012; Noble et al., 2019; Brun-Usan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: Neither of the two scenarios for plasticity-led evolution are likely to apply to the repeated evolution of similar locomotor skeletons in Anolis ecomorphs.
source: The present results suggest that neither of these scenarios are likely to apply to the repeated evolution of similar locomotor skeletons in Anolis ecomorphs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental and comparative results.

claim: The plastic responses to microhabitats do not radically change what phenotypes are available to selection, or which ones are fit.
source: While some microhabitats may rarely be encountered in nature by a given species, our experiments show that the plastic responses to these microhabitats do not radically change what phenotypes are available to selection, or which ones are fit.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing poor alignment between plasticity and performance.

claim: Selection on genetic variation appears sufficient to cause the evolutionary divergence in the locomotor skeleton between ecomorphs.
source: That is, selection on genetic variation appears sufficient to cause the evolutionary divergence in the locomotor skeleton between ecomorphs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of alignment between plasticity and evolutionary divergence.

claim: Anolis lizards have not evolved to exploit the responsiveness of bone growth as a mechanism for adjusting their morphology to the microhabitat in which they happen to be born.
source: Our experiments also suggest that Anolis lizards have not evolved to exploit the responsiveness of bone growth as a mechanism for adjusting their morphology to the microhabitat in which they happen to be born.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that plasticity does not consistently improve performance.

claim: The hallmarks of adaptive plasticity are precise developmental 'switches' or physiological mechanisms that ensure that individuals can adjust their phenotype adaptively and often reversibly.
source: The hallmarks of such adaptive plasticity are precise developmental 'switches' (e.g., seasonal polyphenism in butterflies and other insects; Brakefield, 1996) or physiological mechanisms that ensure that individuals can adjust their phenotype adaptively and often reversibly (e.g., vertebrate stress responses).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on adaptive plasticity.

claim: The flexibility of bone growth in Anolis appears a poor mechanism for adjusting individual morphology to match the local environment.
source: In comparison, the flexibility of bone growth in Anolis appears a poor mechanism for adjusting individual morphology to match the local environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing poor alignment between plasticity and performance.

claim: The developmental mechanisms that underlie species differences in limb length may act very early in development, before any mechanical stress imposed by locomotion.
source: In fact, the developmental mechanisms that underlie species differences in limb length may act very early in development, before any mechanical stress imposed by locomotion (Sanger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous developmental research.

claim: Environmentally induced variation in bone morphology may typically exercise a transient effect on the direction of adaptation to microhabitat.
source: If this is not peculiar to Anolis, environmentally induced variation in bone morphology may typically exercise a transient effect on the direction of adaptation to microhabitat.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the Anolis results.

claim: Comparisons of the relationship between plasticity and adaptive divergence over different time scales will be important to reveal the extent to which plasticity is consequential, and when it facilitates or hampers adaptation.
source: Thus, in general, comparisons of the relationship between plasticity and adaptive divergence over different time scales will be important to reveal the extent to which plasticity is consequential, and when it facilitates or hampers adaptation.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the study's findings.

claim: The locomotor skeleton has evolved within a subset of possible morphologies that are highly accessible through genetic change, allowing repeatability of adaptive divergence independently of plasticity.
source: In conclusion, we reveal a consistent but moderate degree of morphological convergence in the locomotor skeleton of Greater Antillean Anolis. Our comparative and experimental analyses demonstrate that phenotypic plasticity is unlikely to have contributed to the repeated evolution of limb and girdle morphologies in Anolis ecomorphs. Instead, we suggest that the locomotor skeleton has evolved within a subset of possible morphologies that are highly accessible through genetic change, allowing repeatability of adaptive divergence independently of plasticity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all findings.

claim: The study quantified morphology using 18 3D landmarks each on the pectoral and the pelvic girdle.
source: We quantified shape using 18 3D landmarks each on the pectoral and the pelvic girdle (partially adapted from Tinius and Russell, 2014; Tinius et al., 2018; Supplementary file 1A), and measured the length of 15 limb elements of fore- and hindlimb, as well as the cortical thickness and bone diameter in virtual cross-sections of the four long bones (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the morphological measurements taken in the study.

claim: The study measured the length of 15 limb elements of fore- and hindlimb.
source: We quantified shape using 18 3D landmarks each on the pectoral and the pelvic girdle (partially adapted from Tinius and Russell, 2014; Tinius et al., 2018; Supplementary file 1A), and measured the length of 15 limb elements of fore- and hindlimb, as well as the cortical thickness and bone diameter in virtual cross-sections of the four long bones (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the morphological measurements taken in the study.

claim: The study measured cortical thickness and bone diameter in virtual cross-sections of the four long bones.

evidence: This describes the morphological measurements taken in the study.

claim: The centroid size of the pelvic girdle was used as a proxy for body size.
source: We used the centroid size of the pelvic girdle as a proxy for body size.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the study.

claim: The study used micro-CT scans of museum specimens.
source: Using micro-CT scans of museum specimens, we quantified the morphology of the locomotor skeleton of 259 males from 95 Greater Antillean Anolis species that have been assigned to one of six ecomorph categories (Losos, 2009; Nicholson et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the data source for the comparative analysis.

claim: The study quantified the morphology of the locomotor skeleton of 259 males from 95 Greater Antillean Anolis species.
source: Using micro-CT scans of museum specimens, we quantified the morphology of the locomotor skeleton of 259 males from 95 Greater Antillean Anolis species that have been assigned to one of six ecomorph categories (Losos, 2009; Nicholson et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the sample size of the comparative analysis.

claim: The ecomorph classification does not always rely on well-documented habitat use.
source: We acknowledge that the ecomorph classification does not always rely on well-documented habitat use (Poe and Anderson, 2019), but there is a very close concordance between classification based on habitat use (Nicholson et al., 2012) and classification that also includes gross morphology, such as the total length of limbs, head size and tail length (Losos, 2009).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the ecomorph classification system.

claim: There is a very close concordance between ecomorph classification based on habitat use and classification that also includes gross morphology.
source: We acknowledge that the ecomorph classification does not always rely on well-documented habitat use (Poe and Anderson, 2019), but there is a very close concordance between classification based on habitat use (Nicholson et al., 2012) and classification that also includes gross morphology, such as the total length of limbs, head size and tail length (Losos, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous classification studies.

claim: The first principal component explains 16.32% of the variance in the morphological data.
source: (A) The first and second principal components on the level of individual explain 16.32% and 13.00% of the variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the principal component analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second principal component explains 13.00% of the variance in the morphological data.
source: (A) The first and second principal components on the level of individual explain 16.32% and 13.00% of the variance, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the principal component analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The features that load most strongly on PC1 are the shape of the pelvic girdle and humerus length.
source: The features that load most strongly on PC1 are the shape of the pelvic girdle and humerus length, and features loading strongly on PC2 are the shape of the pectoral girdle and bone cortical thickness (Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the principal components.

claim: Features loading strongly on PC2 are the shape of the pectoral girdle and bone cortical thickness.
source: The features that load most strongly on PC1 are the shape of the pelvic girdle and humerus length, and features loading strongly on PC2 are the shape of the pectoral girdle and bone cortical thickness (Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the principal components.

claim: Jamaica and Puerto Rico do not possess the full set of six ecomorphs.
source: Note that Jamaica and Puerto Rico do not possess the full set of six ecomorphs, but lack one and two ecomorphs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1.

claim: Jamaica lacks one ecomorph.
source: Note that Jamaica and Puerto Rico do not possess the full set of six ecomorphs, but lack one and two ecomorphs, respectively.

claim: Puerto Rico lacks two ecomorphs.

claim: Hatchlings of A. sagrei and A. carolinensis were raised in groups of six lizards in structurally different habitats until they reached 5 months of age.
source: Hatchlings of A. sagrei and A. carolinensis were raised in groups of six lizards in structurally different habitats, (A) 'climbing' habitat and (B) 'running' habitat. Animals were reared under these conditions until they reached 5 months of age, at which the majority of animals had reached sexual maturity (images show recently hatched lizards).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of animals had reached sexual maturity at 5 months of age.
source: Hatchlings of A. sagrei and A. carolinensis were raised in groups of six lizards in structurally different habitats, (A) 'climbing' habitat and (B) 'running' habitat. Animals were reared under these conditions until they reached 5 months of age, at which the majority of animals had reached sexual maturity (images show recently hatched lizards).
evidence: This describes the developmental stage at the end of the experiment.

claim: The study raised 45 male lizards of A. carolinensis on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood.
source: To test this hypothesis, we raised 45 male lizards of a trunk-crown (Anolis carolinensis, adapted to climbing) and 71 male lizards of a trunk-ground (A. sagrei, adapted to running) species on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental sample size.

claim: The study raised 71 male lizards of A. sagrei on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood.
source: To test this hypothesis, we raised 45 male lizards of a trunk-crown (Anolis carolinensis, adapted to climbing) and 71 male lizards of a trunk-ground (A. sagrei, adapted to running) species on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental sample size.

claim: A. carolinensis is a trunk-crown species adapted to climbing.
source: To test this hypothesis, we raised 45 male lizards of a trunk-crown (Anolis carolinensis, adapted to climbing) and 71 male lizards of a trunk-ground (A. sagrei, adapted to running) species on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ecology of A. carolinensis.

claim: A. sagrei is a trunk-ground species adapted to running.
source: To test this hypothesis, we raised 45 male lizards of a trunk-crown (Anolis carolinensis, adapted to climbing) and 71 male lizards of a trunk-ground (A. sagrei, adapted to running) species on broad versus narrow surfaces until they reached adulthood (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ecology of A. sagrei.

claim: The differences in the structural habitats promoted different styles of locomotion and perching behaviour.
source: The differences in the structural habitats promoted different styles of locomotion and perching behaviour (Feiner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: Both A. carolinensis and A. sagrei belong to the Cuban clade.
source: Both species belong to the Cuban clade and, therefore, the appropriate evolutionary divergence to compare against is the contrast between the respective ecomorphs in this clade on Cuba (trunk-ground [NIndividuals = 20, NSpecies = 9] versus trunk-crown [NIndividuals = 20, NSpecies = 9]).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic knowledge of Anolis relationships.

claim: The morphology of both A. carolinensis and A. sagrei responded to the microhabitat treatment.
source: The morphology of both species responded to the microhabitat treatment.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing plastic responses.

claim: Among all 132 traits, 15 traits significantly distinguish between Cuban trunk-ground and trunk-crown specimens.
source: Among all 132 traits, we singled out 15 traits that significantly distinguish between Cuban trunk-ground and trunk-crown specimens (i.e., the most evolutionary divergent traits), and 14 and 10 traits that significantly distinguish the environmentally induced microhabitat specialists in A. carolinensis and A. sagrei, respectively (i.e., most plastic traits; see Material and methods).
evidence: This describes the identification of evolutionarily divergent traits.

claim: 14 traits significantly distinguish the environmentally induced microhabitat specialists in A. carolinensis.
source: Among all 132 traits, we singled out 15 traits that significantly distinguish between Cuban trunk-ground and trunk-crown specimens (i.e., the most evolutionary divergent traits), and 14 and 10 traits that significantly distinguish the environmentally induced microhabitat specialists in A. carolinensis and A. sagrei, respectively (i.e., most plastic traits; see Material and methods).
evidence: This describes the identification of plastic traits in A. carolinensis.

claim: 10 traits significantly distinguish the environmentally induced microhabitat specialists in A. sagrei.
source: Among all 132 traits, we singled out 15 traits that significantly distinguish between Cuban trunk-ground and trunk-crown specimens (i.e., the most evolutionary divergent traits), and 14 and 10 traits that significantly distinguish the environmentally induced microhabitat specialists in A. carolinensis and A. sagrei, respectively (i.e., most plastic traits; see Material and methods).
evidence: This describes the identification of plastic traits in A. sagrei.

claim: The most plastic traits showed limited overlap between the three runner/climber contrasts.
source: Notably, these traits showed limited overlap between the three runner/climber contrasts: while A. carolinensis showed the greatest plastic response in the anterior part of the locomotor skeleton, the most affected traits in A. sagrei were found in the posterior part associated with the pelvic girdle or the hindlimb (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the identity of plastic traits across species and evolutionary divergence.

claim: A vector of the 15 traits that show the strongest evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown lizards on Cuba was not significantly aligned with the plasticity vector of A. carolinensis (40.20°).
source: Similarly, a vector of the 15 traits that show the strongest evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown lizards on Cuba was not significantly aligned with the plasticity vector of A. carolinensis (40.20°) or A. sagrei (125.98°; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is supported by calculating angles between vectors of evolutionarily divergent traits and plasticity.

claim: A vector of the 15 traits that show the strongest evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown lizards on Cuba was not significantly aligned with the plasticity vector of A. sagrei (125.98°).
source: Similarly, a vector of the 15 traits that show the strongest evolutionary divergence between trunk-ground and trunk-crown lizards on Cuba was not significantly aligned with the plasticity vector of A. carolinensis (40.20°) or A. sagrei (125.98°; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is supported by calculating angles between vectors of evolutionarily divergent traits and plasticity.

claim: The study performed two trials that capture perching behaviour and locomotor performance in the lizards that were raised in the two microhabitats.
source: To assess how well morphology predicts functional aspects related to fitness, we performed two trials that capture perching behaviour and locomotor performance in the lizards that were raised in the two microhabitats (see Material and methods).
evidence: This describes the behavioral assays conducted in the study.

claim: The repeatability of the landmarking procedure was 0.98 for the pectoral girdle.
source: Using this method, we found that the repeatability of the entire procedure of extracting morphologies and applying landmarks was 0.98 for the pectoral girdle, and 0.94 for the pelvic girdle (Supplementary files 1J and 1K).
evidence: This describes the reliability of the morphological measurements.

claim: The repeatability of the landmarking procedure was 0.94 for the pelvic girdle.
source: Using this method, we found that the repeatability of the entire procedure of extracting morphologies and applying landmarks was 0.98 for the pectoral girdle, and 0.94 for the pelvic girdle (Supplementary files 1J and 1K).
evidence: This describes the reliability of the morphological measurements.

claim: The centroid size of the pelvic girdle was highly correlated with the centroid size of the pectoral girdle (r = 0.99, p-value<0.001, N = 375).
source: The centroid size of the pelvic girdle was highly correlated with the centroid size of the pectoral girdle (r = 0.99, p-value<0.001, N = 375), and with snout-vent length (SVL) measured in lab-reared lizards using a digital caliper (A. carolinensis: r = 0.96, p-value<0.001, N = 45; A. sagrei: r = 0.97, p-value<0.001, N = 71).
evidence: This validates the use of pelvic girdle centroid size as a body size proxy.

evidence: This validates the use of pelvic girdle centroid size as a body size proxy.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.
